https://www.dw.com/en/how-two-wars-and-e.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5HoFl Supplies of rice — consumed by half the world's population — are at risk from El Nino Image: Amit Dave/REUTERS Advertisement A potentially record-strength El Nino is now intensifying across the Pacific, bringing either drought or flooding to the world's key farming regions. Earlier this month, the US National Oceanic & Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) predicted a 63% chance that the unusual weather pattern could be " very strong " this year. JP Morgan, meanwhile, warned last week that El Nino, combined with $100 (€88) oil prices, could spike food inflation by up to 1.5%. The arrival of El Nino follows two major conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, during which global food supplies have held up remarkably well. So, could this third crisis bring the perfect storm that tips the balance? Are African nations underestimating the risks of El Nino? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Triple blow to global food security Russia's war in Ukraine still hangs over one of the world's major grain-exporting regions, where repeated attacks on ports and farmland continue to threaten one of the planet's key breadbaskets. The Iran war has driven up energy and fertilizer prices, raising the cost of growing food worldwide and causing temporary supply disruptions for key soil nutrients. El Nino, which shifts rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide, is expected to be so strong that the World Bank warned recently it could cut rice output by 20% to 50% in affected regions. Maximo Torero, chief economist of the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), warned of a "compound effect" that could create "a very complex situation" by the end of the year. "We are very concerned about El Nino and the delay of the monsoon ... in India ," Torero told DW. El Nino is expected to slow down and weaken India’s monsoon season , a vital time for rice planting. June already saw around 40% less rainfall than normal, according to local media. India produces nearly a third of the world’s rice, the vast majority of which is consumed domestically. Aside from South Asia, the FAO thinks the El Nino risks are highest in Africa's Sahel region , southern Africa , Southeast Asia and in the Dry Corridor of Central America. The UN food agency warned this month that some of these regions face a more than 50% chance of drought in the next few months. World producing more food than ever Despite the geopolitical strife, food prices remain nearly 20% below their 2022 peak, according to the FAO Food Price Index. The world brought in the biggest grain harvest in history last year. This is because farmers planted more land, the weather has been favorable and the crops produced more per acre. While this year is expected to be slightly smaller, the harvest will still be the second-largest ever. “We are seeing improvements in agricultural productivity," Simone Bunse, senior researcher at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), told DW, citing India and Latin America as notable examples. "These have helped sustain food production and reduce undernourishment. And this is balancing some of the localized impacts of conflict.” UN experts expect a 50% chance of drought across much of southern Africa Image: Jekesai Njikizana/AFP/Getty Images Millions still go hungry War is a major barrier to getting hunger under control globally. The UN says 266 million people are still facing acute hunger, more than half of them due to conflict. The worst of it is concentrated in just a handful of conflict-hit countries, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sudan and Yemen, where supplies cannot reach the people who need them. "We have enough calories produced in the world to feed everybody," Torero said. "Those calories are not distributed in the same way across the world, and that's the challenge." War often destroys local food sources, displaces millions of people, damages infrastructure and severely cuts humanitarian access. In some hotspots such as Sudan and Gaza, experts say hunger is increasingly being used as a weapon. "Parties deliberately destroy farmland, livestock, water systems, food storage facilities, and transport routes. They jeopardize access to markets and obstruct humanitarian assistance," SIPRI's Bunse told DW. Farmers pinched by elevated fertilizer prices Another risk to global food supplies is fertilizer , around a third of which normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz . The strait remains heavily disrupted after a failed ceasefire between the US and Iran, along with attacks on shipping in the Red Sea . Some farmers have been paying substantially more for fertilizer, delaying purchases or switching to crops that require less fertiliser . If they ultimately apply less, yields could suffer in the next harvest. Food security experts believe the Middle East conflict alone could leave millions more people hungry by 2030 — and that projection does not yet account for the effects of El Nino. With temperatures in the Pacific Ocean expected to rise by 3.6 degrees Celsius (38.4 degrees Fahrenheit) — almost double the 2015/6 El Nino — climate think tank Berkeley Earth now predicts this year's weather pattern will be strongest on record. If oil prices leap past $120 a barrel again, if grain exports from Ukraine are successfully blocked, or if El Nino bites harder into next year’s crops as farmers plant less, then the world could face a spike in hunger, experts predict. If all of those happen at once, the impact would be far worse, with JP Morgan predicting that food inflation will surpass 5% in 2027 and that emerging markets would take the biggest hit. https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2026/.text: Russia is considering staging a false-flag attack against critical infrastructure in the Baltics using Ukrainian drones in an attempt to discredit Kyiv and weaken NATO's backing for Ukraine, Lithuania's defence minister, Robertas Kaunas, has warned. “We are talking about a potential false-flag operation where a fake Ukrainian drone could be used,” he said during a press briefing. “That’s the most realistic current scenario."For such an attack, parts of Ukrainian drones that were launched against military and energy targets inside Russia could be used.Ukraine has repeatedly launched long-range drone attacks against targets inside Russia. While many reach their intended targets, others are intercepted or crash, leaving wreckage in Russian hands. “[Russia] is capable of assembling them into a functional device, and there is a theoretical possibility that such a device … could be used in a false-flag operation,” Kaunas said. The minister said there is no indication that such an operation is imminent, but that Russia is actively planning scenarios. His warning follows recent reports in Lithuanian media that the country's military intelligence believes Russia is weighing attacks on critical infrastructure across the Baltic region using Ukrainian-made drones. The Baltic country of less than 3 million has stepped up security around key energy infrastructure, such as the Klaipėda liquefied natural gas terminal, the LitPol Link electricity interconnector with Poland near Alytus, a major transformer substation in Alytus district and the Kruonis pumped-storage hydroelectric plant. A bid to undermine NATO supportLithuania has experienced several drone incursions in recent years. Earlier this year, Lithuanian authorities concluded that drones which crashed on its territory were Ukrainian aircraft that had been diverted from their intended routes by Russian electronic systems while carrying out strikes inside Russia. Last year, two Russian drones also crossed into Lithuanian airspace from Belarus before crashing.However, an intentional strike against critical infrastructure would represent a significant escalation. Kremlin needs it, as Russian society is beginning to question “why there are fuel shortages, why warehouses are burning and why Ukrainian drones are flying over Russia," the minister said. "In order to preserve its grip on power and maintain the image of victory, the Russian regime is looking for alternative ways to escalate the situation,” Kaunas said. One of Moscow's objectives, she argued, would be to sow divisions within the alliance and reduce Western military support for Kyiv. "But I can assure you that will not happen," Kaunas said.
